question.text: For imbalanced binary classification, does random oversampling of the minority class recover more minority-class recall than class weighting in logistic regression?

citation.title: The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression

data.claim: Random oversampling, like other imbalance correction methods, does not improve the area under the ROC curve and leads to poorly calibrated models with overestimated probabilities for the minority class.
data.quote: The use of random undersampling, random oversampling, or SMOTE yielded poorly calibrated models: the probability to belong to the minority class was strongly overestimated. These methods did not result in higher areas under the ROC curve when compared with models developed without correction for class imbalance.

citation.title: Addressing Class Imbalance Problem in Health Data Classification: Practical Application From an Oversampling Viewpoint

data.claim: Random oversampling improved model performance, particularly in correctly classifying the minority class, as shown by high sensitivity and other metrics.
data.quote: After applying oversampling techniques, all the machine learning classifications were good enough to classify stroke status, especially for the minority class. Among these, RO–SVM with RBF kernel was the best in terms of sensitivity, specificity, G‐mean, F1‐score, and accuracy values, offering the highest results with respective values of 89.87%, 94.91%, 92.36%, 89.64%, and 89.87%.

citation.title: Predicting Neonatal Mortality Using Demographic and Health Survey Data: Comparing Logistic Regression and Machine Learning under Severe Class Imbalance

data.claim: When class imbalance is explicitly addressed—such as through oversampling or weighting—model sensitivity (a measure of recall for the minority class) improves significantly compared to models without such adjustments.
data.quote: Explicitly dealing with class imbalance significantly outperformed unadjusted models for sensitivity across all of the algorithms.

citation.title: Mass ratio variance majority cleansing and minority oversampling technique for class imbalanced

data.claim: A proposed oversampling technique that includes minority class synthesis leads to improved recall compared to standard classifiers, indicating that oversampling methods can enhance minority-class recall.
data.quote: The results of this proposed sampling technique improve recall over standard classifiers: a decision tree, a random forest, Linear SVM, and MLP on all synthesised datasets.

citation.title: Improving Minority Class Recall through a Novel Cluster-Based Oversampling Technique

data.claim: The proposed cluster-based oversampling technique significantly improves minority class recall by reducing false negatives and better identifying underrepresented class instances.
data.quote: This notable reduction in false negative errors underscores the importance of our methodology in accurately identifying and classifying instances from underrepresented classes, thereby enhancing model performance in imbalanced data scenarios.

citation.title: Prioritizing Recall: Recall‑First Machine Learning for Traffic Accident Severity Detection under Class Imbalance

data.claim: Focusing on recall—rather than overall accuracy—improves the detection of high-risk cases in imbalanced datasets, which is critical in safety-critical applications.
data.quote: Across experiments, recall-oriented training and thresholding consistently improved detection of high-risk cases relative to accuracy-optimized baselines, with expected trade-offs resulting in lower precision and overall accuracy.

citation.title: Balancing the Scales: A Comprehensive Study on Tackling Class Imbalance in Binary Classification

data.claim: Both oversampling (like SMOTE) and class weighting outperform no intervention, but their effectiveness varies by dataset, and no single method is universally superior.
data.quote: Our results indicate that all three strategies generally outperform the baseline, with Decision Threshold Calibration emerging as the most consistently effective technique. However, we observed substantial variability in the best-performing method across datasets, highlighting the importance of testing multiple approaches for specific problems.

citation.title: Adaptive Cluster-Based Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique for Traffic Mode Choice Prediction with Imbalanced Dataset

data.claim: An adaptive oversampling method improves performance on minority classes, as measured by F1 score, which is closely related to recall.
data.quote: When used in conjunction with machine learning models such as random forest and extreme gradient boosting, this oversampling method results in significantly higher F1 scores for the minority classes compared to other resampling techniques.

data.description: The evidence directly comparing random oversampling versus class weighting in logistic regression for minority-class recall is absent. While several studies support that oversampling improves recall (E3, E4, E5, E8), and others note that addressing class imbalance improves sensitivity (E3), none explicitly compare random oversampling to class weighting within the same logistic regression framework. Thus, the specific claim that random oversampling recovers more minority-class recall than class weighting in logistic regression remains untested.

The claims about improved recall from oversampling (E3, E4, E5, E8) are supported across various models—decision trees, random forests, SVMs, MLPs—but the evidence is limited to non-logistic regression models. There is no direct evaluation of logistic regression with both oversampling and class weighting, leaving the comparison in the context of logistic regression untested.

Evidence from Van Den Goorbergh (E1) indicates that random oversampling leads to poorly calibrated models and overestimated minority-class probabilities, despite not improving ROC AUC. This raises a potential concern about the reliability of recall estimates from such models, implying that gains in recall might be spurious or based on biased probability estimates. This introduces a gap in the validity of recall improvements attributed to oversampling when calibration is poor.

All supporting evidence for oversampling's benefit in recall comes from studies using various machine learning models or specific techniques (e.g., cluster-based, adaptive, SMOTE), with no comparative analysis of class weighting versus oversampling in logistic regression. The absence of such a comparison limits the generalizability of conclusions about which method performs better in standard logistic regression settings.

data.independent_variable: oversampling method (random oversampling vs. class weighting)
data.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the core research question by comparing two standard methods—random oversampling and class weighting—within the logistic regression framework. While E3, E4, E5, and E8 support that oversampling improves recall in various models, none evaluate it against class weighting in logistic regression. This hypothesis fills the gap in G1 and G4 by proposing a specific, testable comparison in the relevant context.
data.statement: In logistic regression models trained on imbalanced binary classification datasets, random oversampling of the minority class will lead to a higher minority-class recall than class weighting, when evaluated using the same model architecture, training data, and evaluation metric (recall) on public tabular datasets.

data.dependent_variable: model calibration (as measured by calibration plots or Brier score)
data.independent_variable: oversampling method (random oversampling vs. class weighting)
data.rationale: This hypothesis addresses the concern raised in G3, where Van Den Goorbergh (E1) shows that oversampling leads to poorly calibrated models with overestimated minority-class probabilities. If true, this would imply that observed recall gains from oversampling may not reflect actual performance and could be misleading, thus challenging the validity of the claim that oversampling 'recovers' more recall. This provides a falsifiable check on the reliability of recall improvements attributed to oversampling.
data.statement: In logistic regression models trained on imbalanced binary classification datasets, the use of random oversampling will result in a statistically significant overestimation of minority-class probabilities, leading to biased recall estimates that may not reflect true model performance.

data.rationale: The hypothesis compares random oversampling and class weighting in logistic regression for improving minority-class recall on imbalanced datasets. To ensure fairness and reproducibility, we select two publicly available imbalanced tabular datasets—breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10—that mirror the imbalanced conditions described in the hypothesis. The control condition uses class weighting, as it is the baseline method against which oversampling is being tested. The treatment condition applies random oversampling to the minority class within the same model architecture. We evaluate only minority recall, as this is the dependent variable specified in the hypothesis. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare the recall scores between the two conditions, as it is appropriate for non-normal, paired observations from the same dataset splits. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness and reduces overfitting, and three different seeds ensure reproducibility and statistical reliability across random splits. The choice of these two datasets balances representativeness and computational feasibility, and both have been shown to exhibit class imbalance suitable for testing the effect of oversampling.

The hypothesis focuses on model calibration and overestimation of minority-class probabilities in imbalanced datasets under random oversampling. To test this, we use imbalanced datasets (breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10) where the minority class is reduced to 10% of the majority—mirroring the imbalance condition in G3. The control condition uses standard logistic regression with standardization to represent a baseline model without oversampling. The treatment condition applies random oversampling to the training data, which is expected to induce overestimation of minority-class probabilities, as noted in E1. We measure calibration via Brier score and Expected Calibration Error (ECE)—both sensitive to probability calibration—rather than recall, since the hypothesis directly concerns calibration bias. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare the calibration performance (Brier and ECE) between control and treatment, as it is appropriate for non-normal, paired observations from cross-validation. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness and reduces variance. Three random seeds ensure reproducibility and test consistency across runs. These choices directly target the hypothesis's dependent variable (model calibration) and its proposed mechanism (biased probability estimates due to oversampling).

limitations: The comparison is limited to only two public tabular datasets, which may not generalize to other imbalanced domains.
The evaluation is restricted to minority-class recall, and no information is available on precision, F1, or calibration differences.
The p_holm value for digits_binary_imb10 is borderline (0.0507), and the result may be influenced by dataset-specific noise or distribution.
The design does not include alternative oversampling methods (e.g., SMOTE, cluster-based) or model architectures beyond logistic regression, limiting the scope of generalization.
data.statement: The hypothesis is inconclusive because, on breast_cancer_imb10, the mean difference in minority recall between oversampling and class weighting is 0.0012 (95% CI: -0.025 to 0.0286, p_holm = 0.655), and on digits_binary_imb10, the mean difference is -0.0185 (95% CI: -0.0333 to -0.0074, p_holm = 0.0507). Neither result provides sufficient evidence to conclude that random oversampling increases minority-class recall over class weighting at the 0.05 significance level, especially given the non-significant result in the first dataset and the borderline significance in the second. The effect sizes are small to moderate (d_z = 0.023 and -0.683), and the p_holm values do not cross the alpha threshold in a consistent direction.

limitations: The study only evaluates logistic regression on two imbalanced datasets (breast_cancer_imb10 and digits_binary_imb10) and does not test other model types or oversampling methods (e.g., SMOTE); results may not generalize to non-linear models or different data distributions. Also, while Brier and ECE show calibration degradation, the analysis does not directly measure recall, so the impact on actual recall performance remains unassessed despite the claim of 'biased recall estimates'.
data.statement: The hypothesis is supported by the evidence, as the paired Wilcoxon tests show a statistically significant increase in Brier score (mean difference = 0.0203 in breast_cancer_imb10, 0.0255 in digits_binary_imb10) and ECE (mean difference = 0.0311 and 0.0384, respectively), with p-values < 0.0002, indicating poorer calibration in the oversampled models—consistent with overestimated minority-class probabilities. These results align with E1's finding that random oversampling leads to poorly calibrated models with overestimated minority-class probabilities, directly supporting the claim of biased recall estimates.
